A friend if mine, who is a oldschool redneck from east Texas, loves pocket knives and got a Benchmade 940-1 that uses S90V and god damn is it one of the most consistently sharp pocket knives I've ever held. I've seen straight razors that are more dull. It costs like $240 and takes incredibly patience to sharpen, but once you sharpen the thing it *stays* sharp for ages.

That aside, the aluminum handle is bad for a couple of reasons. It's profile is that of a full tang knife which would give it balance, durability, and weight, but since the handle is hollow it gets none of those benefits. First off, make sure you season your cast iron well. Like, really season that bitch. In one day of seasoning I went from a shitty cast iron that every stuck to and about a half inch of carbon buildup on the sides to a beautiful smooth cast iron that eggs slide around in even without oil (though you should definitely use oil)

No matter where you're cooking it, make sure you have the right material for your tools. Plastic is great, but my go-to is a flat top wooden spoon (sometimes called a wooden turner) for my eggs because it's amazing for making scrambled eggs and since its wood it'll never get hot until it's on fire. And if you season your cast iron well you'll never need a spatula for your eggs unless you want them over easy. If that's your bag bring a spatula.

If you've never put tahin on eggs you're missing out. It's amazing. 

Butter us waaaaay better than oil when you're cooking eggs too. It gives them a nice rich, nutty flavor. 

If you're also cooking bacon, cook them together or at least cook the bacon then the eggs, the bacon fat is great for the eggs and even better for the cast iron!

If you need help seasoning your cast iron well, theres a great walkthrough in the sidebar of a popular online community for cast iron enthusiasts that is perfect. And if you're cast iron is really bad and you need to nearly strip it, SOS pads are your friend. If it can't be cleaned by an SOS pad and lots of elbow grease then it was not meant to be clean

Same with cooking.

I've ran kitchens for years now and I've had so many people who love cooking at home try to make a career out of it. It's usually a house wife/husband or a young person who went to culinary school (some bs like a local culinary institute) because they didn't know what else to do.

If I need bodies and it's the slow season I'll give them a shot on garde manger because it's easy and they can get trained up. 9 times out of 10 they realize that cooking at home is fun and easy and chill whereas kitchens can be incredibly stressful and fast and frustrating.

I got a couple of pretty good cooks out of it and one that was my star. She was a mid 40s housewife from a specific country who just needed something to get out of the house. She struggled hard at first but picked up quick and ended up being one of the best cooks I ever had. Always very upbeat, did her job so well and on time that I never even looked at her station, was always willing to help other stations that would struggle with prep, and never touched drugs (except the occasional blunt) and drank only rarely. We'd all go out to a nearby bar after a real shit shift and she'd usually tag along but would just get soda or tea to hang out unless we were celebrating or it was once in a blue moon.

I don't think I'll ever find another like her.

It's a love-hate thing tbh. I've been working in kitchens since I was 16 and I absolutely love cooking, even professionally, but I also hate it because of how stressed it makes me on a daily basis.
